nodes.body: The lost-property room at Silverdale Academy is a cupboard under the main stairs. On the last day of term, everything is tipped out onto three tables in the hall. Anything not claimed by four o'clock will be given to the charity shop. You are helping Mr Okonkwo, the caretaker, sort through a crate of pencil cases and single gloves. Your fingers find something cold at the bottom. It is a brass swimming medal, heavy for its size. The name on the back has been filed off. Only a ghost of the letters is left. The ribbon is long gone. Inside the clasp, scratched so faintly you must hold it to the light, are the numbers 06-07 and a small diving swallow.

choices.label: Look inside the medal's presentation case.

nodes.body: The medal sits in a blue velvet case so old the lid hinge is soft as felt. Tucked into the lining, folded into eighths, is a paper card from a gala. The ink is spidery fountain-pen blue. It says SILVERDALE SWIMMING CLUB CHAMPIONSHIP. Below that are six event names from a club that only half exists any more. The last event listed is RELAY. Below that, a row of six times have been written in and four crossed out. Mr Okonkwo turns the case over in his hands. He says it came out of a locker. The locker has not been opened since before the pool roof was fixed. He says the boy who used it swam for the old town club.

choices.label: Ask Mr Okonkwo about the locker.
Start at the nearest event on the list.
Take the fixture card to the school office.

nodes.body: Mr Okonkwo has cleared a dozen lockers this term. He remembers every one, including the names that were still on the backs. The locker with the medal belonged to a boy called Harry Vance. He left in March, two years ago. A whole carrier bag of his things sits in the caretaker's office. Nobody has put it into the charity pile yet because the bag is still taped shut.

choices.label: Ask to see the taped-up bag.

nodes.body: Held up to the light, the swallow on the clasp points toward the pool. The six events sit along an unseen line that runs from the shallow end to the deep end. The nearest is the old starting blocks. They are now just a stack of plastic chairs stored where the diving boards used to be. The deep end has been a storage bay since before you started school.

nodes.body: The school office keeps the club's old records in two filing cabinets. They also have a computer that runs a sign-up system nobody has used for years. Priya works at the front desk. Eleven swimmers borrow a relay cup. They use a photocopied map and six brass plates. The team stops at all six points in the heat and races badly at each one. More people follow it round than anyone expected, and half of them are under twelve.

Forty people walk the route on a September Saturday. A woman of seventy-nine leads them. She stops at each plate and says what happened there. At the starting-block store, there is no plate at all. But everybody stands in the changing-room hall and listens anyway.

Five plates go back onto five walls with the right screws. A man on the industrial estate cuts the sixth one new in brass. He will not take money for it. It goes onto the starting-block store wall. It fits a rectangle that has been waiting for twenty years.

The medal goes back into the case with the card folded beside it. It lives on a shelf, polished once a month. It is the only object in the story that ends up exactly where it started. And now it means something completely different.

ending.title: Six Plates Back on Six Walls

nodes.body: Trophies go to the PE department, paper to the school office, a photo to the pool house. Plates go to the walls and the card to the archive with a note saying who found it. It takes three weeks of small dull errands. In the end, nothing is left in a bag under anybody's bed.

The cabinet comes out onto the floor. It gets listed, photographed, and split into keep and skip. This happens in front of the driver. He is paid by the hour and is quite keen. The space under the trophy display ends the day swept, dry and empty.

The skip leaves the loading bay at quarter past four. A relay cup and four medal cases are inside it. Someone takes a photo of it going from the gate. The bulletin won't print the picture because there is nothing to say about it.
Three separate adults would have stopped it, but no one told them. Asking felt like a bigger thing at lunchtime than it turned out to be. On the next Monday, all three said so, one after the other.

The last order is wrong and the wheels go back to zero. A trail ran from a crate under the stairs, through six walls and twenty years. It ends at a steel door in a cold hall with a van booked for four o'clock.

ending.title: The Trail Ends at a Steel Door
